title: Old Savoy church bell to be moved to school
text:
The Savoy Methodist Church, above left, now vacant, on Fowler street. Savoy ISD Superintendent Brian Neal, above right, sits on a pew in the old Methodist Church, property of the School District. The 1878 church bell, below left, as it looks today. Nancy Savoy with her late husband, John Savoy, below right, at a Victorian Ball in Phoenix.

Old Savoy church bell to be moved to school

BY VICKI GRAVES
BONHAM DEMOCRAT

SAVOY — The sound of the great, old church bell calling the Methodist congregation to worship won't leave Savoy. But the bell will be moved from the church to the school.

The relocation is being made possible by a heroine from Arizona, Savoy Independent School District Superintendent Brian Neal said Wednesday.

Nancy Savoy, wife of the late John Savoy — the last remaining grandson of Col. William Savoy who founded the town, recently gave $25,000 to Savoy ISD. With the money, Neal will remove and restore the bell and establish a $1,000 annual scholarship. Savoy ISD will sell the church building.

Col. Savoy donated the land for the 1878 church on Fowler Street. Long ago, the congregation blended with another church and the school district came into possession of the building. In the years that followed, the local opry played there, but the building gradually deteriorated, Neal said.

"It's the oldest building in Savoy, to my knowledge, and one of the only buildings that survived the 1878 tornado. It was a new building at the time and the city documents that it was used as a morgue. Over the years, the foundation sunk, and last year we closed it."

Neal said some of the Savoy family members returned and kind of discovered Savoy for themselves a few years ago, renewing ties to the community. At that time, local people made Nancy Savoy aware of the plight of the church. She wanted to buy and restore the whole building, but that was going to be really expensive," said Neal, "and even then, we don't have the money to maintain it. I don't have the money to pay the electric bill."

The school district is never going to be able to restore the church building, but Neal doesn't want to tear it down. He fears, however, that if he doesn't do something soon, he'll have to demolish it in five years. The building is in pretty good shape, but the foundation has rotted, he said, adding, "the Bois d' Arc is still there but the pecan timbers are gone."

The inscription on the bell's side says it was made by Henry McShane, Baltimore, Maryland. Neal thinks it weighs 2,000 pounds and he knows it's five feet tall. He has been in the bell tower.

"I've rung it a time or two, and the manufacturer and the year '1878' is right there on it," he said. "We called and the manufacturer is still in business. They still make bells. They pulled their file and told us when it was ordered and that it cost $40."
